20      I.         INTRODUCTION
21           By way of the instant motion in limine, Plaintiff SANTIAGO TALAVERA
22   CASTRO (“Plaintiff”) seeks an order excluding any evidence (whether by way of
23   document or testimony), discussion, or arguments concerning the availability of
24   arbitration as an alternative to the instant litigation. Such evidence is irrelevant and
25   would create unnecessary consumption of time (i.e., having to explain why Plaintiff did
26   not resort to such processes), confusion of the issues (i.e., holding Plaintiff responsible
27   for filing the instant lawsuit and forcing the jury into jury service instead of resorting to
28   arbitration), and would cause undue prejudice (including forcing Plaintiff to potentially
                                                    3

               Case 5:24-cv-06274-NW     Document 75     Filed 05/01/26   Page 4 of 43




 1   disclose privileged communications concerning the difference between arbitration or
 2   litigation).
 3      II.      ANTICIPATED EVIDENCE
 4            It is anticipated that Defendant FCA US LLC would seek to introduce evidence
 5   that it participates in an arbitration program—through the California Department of
 6   Consumer Affairs’ Certified Arbitration Programs—that would be an alternative to the
 7   instant litigation.
 8      III.     THE EVIDENCE IS INADMISSIBLE
 9            Evidence is relevant only if it has any tendency to make a fact more or less
10   probably and that fact is of consequence in determining the action. Fed. R. Evid., Rule
11   401. Evidence that is irrelevant is inadmissible. Fed. R. Evid., Rule 402.
12            Under the construct of the Song-Beverly, evidence of such alternative dispute
13   resolution programs are only relevant as a defense to “non-willful” civil penalties under
14   California Civil Code §1794(e). However, Plaintiff does not seek civil penalties under
15   such provision—Plaintiff seeks civil penalties under California Civil Code §1794(c),
16   which requires a showing of willfulness. See, Suman v. BMW of N. Am., Inc. (1994) 23
17   Cal.App.4th 1 (acknowledging the two different means of obtaining civil penalty
18   damages).
19            The Act does not “require consumers to take any affirmative steps to secure relief
20   for the failure of a manufacturer to service or repair a vehicle to conform to applicable
21   warranties-other than, of course, permitting the manufacturer a reasonable opportunity to
22   repair the vehicle.” Krotin v. Porsche Cars North America, Inc. (1995) 38 Cal.App.4th
23   294, 302-303. The “Act creates an affirmative duty upon the manufacturer…to provide
24   restitution or replacement when a…nonconformity is not repaired after a reasonable
25   number of attempts.” Krotin, supra, at 301-302. See also, Lukather v. General Motors
26   LLC (2010) 181 Cal.App.4th 1041, 1049.
27            “If the jury chooses to impose a penalty, the amount may be up to two times the
28   amount of damages . . . . There is no definite or required method of determining a

                                                     4
                                    JOINT MOTIONS IN LIMINE DOCUMENT
            Case 5:24-cv-06274-NW        Document 75     Filed 05/01/26    Page 5 of 43




 1   penalty nor is the opinion of a witness required as to the amount of a penalty.” Suman v.
 2   Superior Court (1995) 39 Cal.App.4th 1309, 1323.
 3         Hence, the focus at trial will be whether Defendant had “good faith and reasonable
 4   belief” in its denial of Plaintiff’s reimbursement request, and NOT whether Defendant
 5   was reasonable in providing alternate avenues of resolution, such as an arbitration
 6   program. As such, any arbitration evidence would be irrelevant to the case at bar and
 7   should be excluded.
 8         Moreover, even if there is a modicum of relevance of this evidence, the risk of
 9   unfair prejudice, confusing the issues, misleading the jury, undue delay substantially
10   outweigh such relevance. Fed. R. Evid., Rule 403. Simply put, whether a consumer
11   elects to file with the Court or an arbitration forum is irrelevant to questions of liability
12   here and may also implicate (and force disclosure of) privileged communications.
13         Admission of evidence a proposed arbitration would completely mislead the jury
14   as to what action Defendant is obligated to take under the Act. As stated, Defendant has
15   an affirmative duty under the Act to promptly replace the Subject Vehicle, or make
16   restitution, when it is unable to conform the vehicle to warranty. Defendant cannot now
17   avoid its duty by simply proposing that Plaintiff agree to arbitration. By seeking to
18   inform the jury that it offered, and Plaintiff subsequently declined, arbitration, Defendant
19   undoubtedly hopes to influence the jury by “muddying the waters” of what it was legally
20   obligated to do. The jury would likely be improperly misled into thinking that Defendant
21   is not only required to offer arbitration, but that arbitration is one avenue a manufacturer
22   may take in an effort to comply with its legal obligations and avoid liability at trial. The
23   jury must not be misled into believing such notions are correct.
24         By allowing Defendant to introduce evidence, argument, or reference to the
25   Arbitration Programs, the jury may also receive the impression that Plaintiff could or
26   should have exercised Plaintiff’s right to proceed to arbitration rather than a jury trial.
27   Defendant also frequently attempts to argue that arbitration is a more superior,
28   expeditious process to a civil jury trial. However, the efficiency of alternative dispute

 1   resolution is not a matter to be considered by the jury. Obviously, a civil jury trial is a
 2   fundamental right guaranteed under both the United States and California Constitutions.
 3   Plaintiff should not be prejudiced, maligned, or besmirched for choosing to exercise
 4   those rights.
 5          Introducing evidence or argument about arbitration unnecessarily confuses the
 6   issues, prejudices the Plaintiff, and has the potential to mislead the jury. There is no
 7   obligation for a consumer to go through nonbinding arbitration. Were this to become an
 8   issue at trial, it would confuse the burden. It would necessitate considerable time to go
 9   through the details of Defendant’s program’s compliance with subdivision (1) through
10   (9) of Civil Code § 1793.22(d) and the requirements of 16 C.F.R. §§ 7031.1, 703.2,
11   703.3, 703.4, 703.5, 703.6, 703.7 and 703.8. A program would need to be shown to
12   provide any and all remedies permitted by statute. By extension, the program could not
13   allow any offset but that permitted by Cal. Civ. Code 1793.2(d)(2)(C). See, Jiagbogu v.
14   Mercedes-Benz USA (2004) 118 Cal.App.4th 1235, 1243-1244. The issues would,
15   frankly, result in a time sink where Plaintiffs are not seeking a remedy under Cal. Civ.
16   Code 1794(e). Therefore, all references to the Arbitration Programs should be excluded
17   at trial

23                Warranty
24         The Song-Beverly Act applies a two-part test to the question of whether a vehicle
25   qualifies for repurchase: (1) the vehicle has a nonconformity to warranty; and (2) the
26   manufacturer or its representative is unable to properly repair it after “a reasonable number
27   of attempts.” (Civ. Code, § 1793.2 [emphasis added].)

 6   4th 785, 799, “The reasonableness of the number of repair attempts is a question of fact
 7   to be determined in light of the circumstances”).
 8         To constitute a repair opportunity, the dealership need not have verified, nor even
 9   tried to repair the problem; what matters is the number of opportunities or presentations
10   to conduct a repair, not whether Defendant made use of them. (Oregel v. American Isuzu
11   Motors, Inc. (2001) 90 Cal.App.4th 1094, 1103-1104; Schreidel v. American Honda
12   Motor Co. (1995) 34 Cal. App. 4th 1242, 1253, “Honda claims the record shows that its
13   mechanics were unable to duplicate the problems Schreidel described…”).
14         Courts look to whether the entire vehicle (not just a particular component) was
15   conformed to warranty. “The statute requires the manufacturer to afford the specified
16   remedies of restitution or replacement if that manufacturer is unable to repair the vehicle
17   ‘after a reasonable number of attempts.’” (Silvio v. Ford Motor Company (2003) 109
18   Cal.App.4th 1205, 1208 (emphasis added); “[T]he only affirmative step the Act imposes
19   on consumers is to permit the manufacturer a reasonable opportunity to repair the vehicle.
20   Whether or not the manufacturer's agents choose to take advantage of the opportunity or
21   are unable despite that opportunity to isolate and make an effort to repair the problem, are
22   matters for which the consumer is not responsible” (Oregel. 90 Cal.App.4th at 1103-
23   1104).
